The ledgers lived in the bottom drawer of the filing cabinet, eleven of them, bound in green cloth that had gone the color of seaweed at the spines. Wren had always thought of them as her father's diaries. She had never opened one without his permission, not even after she took over the daily books at nineteen and he kept the master accounts for himself.

That night, after the last crossing, she took out the newest one and opened it on the desk.

The first pages were what she expected. Fuel. Wages for Jonah Marsh, the deckhand, paid every Friday in cash. Insurance. Harbor dues to Ada's office. Her father's handwriting was small and upright and ruthless about decimal points.

Then, in the autumn of last year, the handwriting changed.

It was still his, but it leaned. It pressed harder. And the entries were different. *Received, Pell Coastal Holdings, $40,000.* Then, a month later, *Received, Pell Coastal Holdings, $25,000.* Then a third, and a fourth. Beside each one, in the margin, a small mark she didn't recognize: a hook, like the curl of a wave.

Wren went to the filing cabinet and pulled the folder marked *Loans*, which she had assumed held the old boatyard note from 1979. It did. It also held a contract on heavy cream paper with an embossed seal: a promissory note between Elias Halloway, sole proprietor, Halloway Ferry Service, and Pell Coastal Holdings of Portland. One hundred and twenty thousand dollars. Secured against the property known as Halloway Pier and associated waterfront parcels. Payment in full due the thirtieth of June, 1987.

She read it three times. Then she sat down on the floor of the office because her legs had stopped consulting her.

A hundred and twenty thousand dollars. The ferry cleared perhaps nine thousand in a good year. Her father had borrowed the pier, the pier his own father had driven pilings for in 1931, from a company she had never heard of, and he had told no one. Not her. Not Ada. And then he had gone out alone into Gullet Sound in the March dark and not come back.

She made herself get up. She made herself go back to the desk. A bookkeeper does not sit on floors.

She turned the ledger over to look for anything else he might have hidden in it, and that was when she felt the lump in the back cover. Under the endpaper, someone had cut a careful slit and slid something flat inside. She worked it out with the letter opener.

A key. Small, brass, old, the teeth worn smooth. A paper tag was tied to it with red thread, and on the tag, in her father's leaning hand, two words: *Box 14.*

Wren turned it over in her palm. It was too small for a door. Too plain for a car. A post office box, maybe, or a safe deposit box at the Saltmarsh Savings and Loan, or a locker at the boatyard. Her father had not been a man who locked things. He had left the office door open for forty years.

So whatever Box 14 held, he had wanted it kept from somebody.

*I'll find it,* she told him, the way she had been talking to him for seven weeks, out loud and in her head. *Whatever it is, I'll find it, and then you're going to explain yourself.*

She put the key in the pocket of her cardigan, where she could feel it against her hip, and she sat with the open ledger until the lamp began to flicker. Outside, the tide was coming in under the pier, sucking and sighing at the pilings, and for the first time in her life the sound did not comfort her. It sounded like something counting.
